query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a singular thermomechanical processing step that produces a hierarchical lamellar architecture with graded or interpenetrating lamellar spacing in eutectic high‐entropy alloys will simultaneously improve room-temperature tensile strength and ductility by deflecting microcrack propagation and enabling more uniform plastic deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high‐entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies featuring uniform lamellar spacing and numerous internal boundaries prone to microcrack initiation.
generation.intervention: Apply a tailored thermomechanical processing route to generate a hierarchical lamellar architecture with graded interlamellar spacing (or interpenetrating networks) in the alloy.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation of the eutectic HEA; processing performed under conditions that allow controlled refinement and spatial variation of lamellar spacing.
generation.structural_mediator: A graded lamellar structure that transitions from closely spaced lamellae (to restrict dislocation motion and enhance strength) to more widely spaced regions (to distribute strain uniformly and delay crack growth).
generation.mechanism: The graded lamellar architecture acts to blunt or deflect crack propagation along internal boundaries while facilitating uniform strain distribution during tensile loading, thereby increasing both strength (by refining load-bearing paths and suppressing localized stress concentrations) and ductility (by delaying catastrophic microcrack coalescence).
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified uniform lamellar structure, the engineered hierarchical architecture is expected to exhibit higher yield and ultimate tensile strengths together with an improved tensile elongation at room temperature.
generation.baseline: Eutectic HEAs with conventional, uniformly spaced lamellar colonies that tend to initiate microcracks at internal boundaries under tensile deformation.
generation.boundary: This approach is applicable to eutectic HEAs exhibiting dual-phase lamellar microstructures; its effectiveness may be limited if the fundamental phase composition or interfacial characteristics are significantly altered by other alloying or processing parameters.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of strength and ductility enhancement is uncertain and will depend on the precise control of the graded architecture; experimental validation is required to quantify the improvements.

falsification_experiment.design: Process a batch of the baseline eutectic HEA specimens using the proposed thermomechanical route to generate a hierarchical lamellar architecture. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests on both processed and unprocessed specimens. Use microscopy (e.g., SEM, TEM) to verify the graded lamellar structure and monitor crack initiation and propagation during deformation.
measurements: Crack initiation sites and propagation paths (via in situ imaging)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed specimens do not show statistically significant improvements (e.g., >10% increase) in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the uniform baseline, or if microscopy reveals no meaningful change in crack deflection behavior, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, with an fcc/B2 dual-phase constitution and a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure, exhibited the combination of both high fracture strength and high ductility, which has never been achieved in previously reported HEAs. The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. We choose to not to call it the yield stress, as the mechanism for such a low elastic limit is still unclear at this stage.) of 75 MPa but reaching the fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa. At elevated temperatures of 600 and 700°C (Fig. 4b), the proof stress, fracture stress and elongation were 95 MPa, 806 MPa, 33.7%, and 108 MPa, 538 MPa, 22.9%, respectively, both in the true stress/strain condition. In another study by Gwalani et al., FCC solid solution of Al0.3CoCrFeNi was tailored to produce triplex microstructure containing FCC, B2 and sigma via thermomechanical processing which resulted in a 400% increase in yield strength. Fu et al. studied the effect of Ti addition on Al0.6CoNiFe and they reported a high compressive yield stress of 2200 MPa and 6.2% ductility for spark plasma sintered Al0.6CoFeNi. The microstructure consisted of a mixture of ultra-fine FCC and BCC grains along with L12 precipitates in FCC phase. Addition of even higher amounts of Al in 3d transition element-based high entropy alloys (HEAs) can result in a eutectic FCC/B2 + BCC lamellar microstructure, which can also be rationalized based on the inability of a single FCC phase accommodating a high Al content. frame.system: Eutectic high‐entropy alloys that form dual‐phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries (the starting state), which are prone to microcracking under tensile deformation.
frame.goal: To achieve a single processing or microstructural intervention that simultaneously improves both the strength and the room-temperature tensile ductility of these alloys.
frame.limitation: Conventional processing and previously proposed microstructural-design strategies typically trade off ductility for strength, resulting in brittle failure due to microcrack initiation at the numerous internal boundaries.
root_cause_cues: conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility
constraints: The intervention must be singular (a single processing or design change).
It must operate under room-temperature tensile conditions.
It should overcome the inherent brittleness without resorting to multi-step or highly complex processing techniques.
prior_attempts: Conventional processing methods that improve strength but reduce ductility.
Various microstructural-design and processing strategies that have been attempted but have not eliminated room-temperature brittleness.

families.principle: Engineering the spatial arrangement and geometric parameters of the dual-phase lamellar structure (such as lamellar spacing, colony size, and orientation) can effectively deflect or blunt crack propagation while optimizing load sharing to improve ductility and strength.
cues_for: the trade-off in conventional processing between strength and ductility
cues_against: Existing microstructural-design strategies have been insufficient, suggesting that mere refinement may not be enough unless a new architectural paradigm is introduced
families.best_lever: Design a hierarchical lamellar architecture with graded spacing or interpenetrating networks that both inhibit crack propagation and enable uniform plastic deformation.

families.principle: Directly modifying or reinforcing the interfaces within the lamellar colonies (e.g., by depositing nano-scale coatings or promoting selective interfacial segregation) can reduce stress concentrations and delay microcrack nucleation, thereby improving ductility without sacrificing strength.
cues_for: microcracking initiation at those boundaries under tensile deformation
cues_against: The intervention must be singular and must work under room-temperature conditions; engineering buried interfaces uniformly is challenging
Previous microstructural-design strategies have not fully resolved the brittleness issue
families.best_lever: Introduce a targeted interfacial modification, such as grain-boundary doping or nano-coating deposition, that reinforces the internal boundaries to blunt crack initiation and propagation.

families.principle: Altering the alloy chemistry can modify phase stability, interfacial bonding, and promote beneficial segregation at interfaces, thereby potentially toughening the boundaries while maintaining or increasing strength.
cues_against: Conventional processing methods typically alter mechanics via microstructure rather than composition
Previous strategies focused on microstructural-design or processing, not on intrinsic alloy composition
families.best_lever: Introduce a minor alloying element that segregates to colony boundaries to strengthen interfacial bonding and arrest microcrack propagation.

families.principle: Changing the synthesis route (such as employing rapid or directional solidification) can lead to non-equilibrium microstructures that differ from conventional processing, potentially refining the lamellar colony morphology beneficially.
cues_for: the need for a singular intervention that simultaneously impacts strength and ductility
limitations of conventional processing that inherently trade off ductility for strength
cues_against: Prior attempts with conventional processing have already been exhausted
Synthesis routes might only impact overall morphology and not the internal boundary characteristics in a targeted way
families.best_lever: Develop a novel solidification method that yields a refined lamellar spacing and more continuous phase connectivity, thereby mitigating stress concentration at colony boundaries.

families.principle: Tailored heat treatments or controlled thermomechanical cycles can induce phase transformations, density changes, or precipitation at interfaces that improve both the strength and ductility of multiphase alloys.
cues_for: the question identifies conventional processing methods as raising strength at the expense of ductility
room-temperature tensile conditions imply that any strengthening and ductility improvement must be thermally stable

families.best_lever: Apply a controlled thermomechanical treatment that triggers a subtle precipitation at the lamellar interfaces, thereby enhancing interfacial strength and promoting ductile deformation mechanisms.
